title: Conservatory heritage designation and affordable housing incentives
subtitle: Also: 601 Scottsdale student housing approval, Ontario Reformatory heritage district plan recessed, development charges by-law update.
overview: Council narrowed the heritage designation of the University of Guelph's Rutherford Conservatory at 37 Christie Lane to its salvageable steel elements, after the university said the structure is unsafe and too costly to rebuild. Notice of intention to designate was approved {{vote:m9}}. The university committed to a commemorative garden reusing what it can.

Council received the draft Affordable Housing Community Improvement Plan {{vote:m10}}, with a final report due in January. It also asked staff to consider the feasibility of a property tax deferral program and a fee deferral program for non-profit affordable housing developers {{vote:m13}} {{vote:m14}}. Council approved official plan and zoning changes for two seven-storey student residence buildings at 601 Scottsdale Drive {{vote:m15}}, and adopted development charges by-law updates for Bill 185 on the consent agenda {{vote:m3}}.

The draft Ontario Reformatory Heritage Conservation District plan drew many delegates, most asking for stronger protections. Council recessed late at night before finishing the item, with the motion to receive the report still pending {{vote:m21}}. After an earlier closed session, the Mayor reported that Council received information and gave staff direction on the Public Space Use By-law update. After a later closed session, Council gave staff direction about the reformatory lands.

decisions.detail: Council authorized notice of intention to designate the conservatory, with heritage attributes limited to salvageable steel elements, and the by-law to return if no objections are received.
Council amended the designation to cover only salvageable steel elements of the conservatory structure {{vote:m8}}.
Council received the draft plan and public feedback, with a final recommendation to come back to Council in January.
Staff will consider the feasibility of a tax increment financing deferral program for non-profit affordable home ownership projects as part of the Affordable Housing Strategy.
Staff will consider the feasibility of a no-interest deferral of application and permit fees until building permit issuance for non-profit affordable housing developers.
Council approved the official plan and zoning amendments allowing two seven-storey residential buildings with 489 suites, rejecting a request from the applicant to defer a decision.
Council approved the Bill 185 amendment memorandum, updated growth-related capital projects and two by-laws as part of the consent agenda.
Council authorized notice of intention to designate the property under the Ontario Heritage Act.

debate: On the conservatory, staff said it met eight of nine heritage criteria and is at risk of collapse. The university said engineers found a full rebuild is needed, at a cost of at least $5 million, and that this competes with student housing and other priorities.

Councillors who supported limiting the designation to salvageable steel said it keeps a city record and commemoration without forcing a rebuild. One councillor argued the university should decide how much steel is reused. Others said that would effectively end the designation, and the amendment was ruled out of order.

On the housing plan, delegates and one councillor raised concerns that the provincial affordability benchmarks are out of reach for low-income residents. They also said 25-year affordability terms are too short, and that public money should go to non-profit and co-operative housing. A landlord asked that the three-unit minimum for the accessory dwelling stream be removed, and staff said they would look at that.

On 601 Scottsdale, the applicant argued that student housing is exempt from Planning Act approvals under Bill 185 and asked Council not to decide. Staff and councillors noted it is a private developer's project on university land. A councillor also said the applicant's claims about exemptions were not settled.

On the reformatory lands, delegates said the plan's wording is weak, citing words like "encourage" and "where possible", and that it defers tree protection to other by-laws. Some said the public had too little time to review it, and others raised errors in the document. Staff said consultation is still to come and that they would review the language.
